transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-04 15:30 UTC
Duration: 52m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Priya (Nebula ML), Omar (Nebula Infra), Lena (Nebula CTO)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive on how sequence length distribution impacts kernel selection and CUDA-graph behavior across TensorRT-LLM and vLLM execution paths. Customer is evaluating on-prem VPC deployment; major concerns around 95th/99th latency tail, KV-cache priming, and when quantized kernels diverge.

Topics covered:
- sequence length scaling, short vs long tails
- kernel sensitivity and path flapping
- CUDA graphs replay stability for mixed-length workloads
- KV cache priming / prefix caching behavior
- batching heuristics and latency SLOs
- quantization edge effects (4-bit vs 8-bit)
- VPC/on-prem networking and NVLink multi-gpu impacts

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: alright, hey everybody, thanks for joining. Um, quick intros, and then Carlos will jump in on the profiling outputs we pulled together.
[00:12] Priya: hey, thanks. We mainly want to understand why our 99th keeps spiking when sequence length jumps from 64 to 256 intermittently. We're seeing kernel path changes and sometimes a cuda graph replay failure.
[00:25] Carlos: cool, that's exactly what we instrumented for. Quick note, some of the labels in the traces are slightly off — the profiler maps show "trtllm_exec" but that covers a few underlying kernel families.
[00:38] Omar: we run on-prem, DGX-ish nodes, mix of A100 and A800 for trials, and we have NVLink across two boxes. VPC-ish network overlay but it's all customer-managed. Security is a big deal so we need to avoid shared-host surprises.
[00:52] Maya: great, candidate goal is to hit 95th < 120ms for the short tail and 99th < 340ms for long tails if possible.
[01:05] Priya: correct, and cost isn't infinite; leaning toward quantized inference if it doesn't break quality.
[01:12] Carlos: ok jumping in — we ran two variants: TRT-LLM with TF32/native TensorRT kernels and vLLM with the dynamic CUDA kernels. Short summary: TRT-LLM picks a smaller set of fused, high-throughput kernels for common seq=64 paths. vLLM maintains a more dynamic dispatch and sometimes stays on a different kernel family for seq>128 which increases latency but lowers memory churn.
[01:38] Carlos: one interesting behavior — when the workload mixes short and long sequences, CUDA graphs replay on TRT path often gets invalidated due to differing launch params, causing a graph recompile or fallback which is expensive. vLLM avoids some recompiles by not capturing a single graph for mixed shapes, but then doesn't get the same steady-state throughput.
[02:10] Lena: when you say "graph invalidation" is that the cudaGraph launch failing or are you seeing fallback to kernel launch instead?
[02:17] Carlos: both. We see a couple of modes: 1) graph replay throws an error and triggers a fallback to immediate-mode kernel launches (high latency spike), 2) the graph is recreated which causes a brief pause while it compiles. Often it's tied to sequence-length variance and KV-cache size changes.
[02:33] Priya: we do a lot of priming — users often start with a short system prompt then long user messages. So the prefix length grows during the session; KV cache size jumps mid-stream.
[02:44] Carlos: exactly, KV cache priming is the other axis. TRT's kernel selector assumes a stable attn/cache footprint; when the KV dims change it can flip to a different kernel (e.g., switch from fused attention to split attention path). That flip is the kernel sensitivity event.
[03:00] Omar: is that flip deterministic? Like do we see it at the same sequence thresholds always?
[03:06] Carlos: mostly, but it depends on memory pressure and prior batches. We have thresholds that look like seq<=96 pick kernel A, seq>96 pick kernel B on some builds, but with quantization or lower workspace memory it shifts. Also the quantized path introduces different tiling so cutover points move.
[03:26] Priya: hm. We tried static batching with max_len=256 and pad, but that wastes memory and increases cost. Any suggestions?
[03:33] Carlos: a few patterns: 1) adaptive bucketing — keep buckets at 32/64/128/256, route to a lane with pinned kernel so graphs are stable per-bucket; 2) prefix-aware caching — don't flush graphs when KV cache grows predictably; 3) for on-prem NVLink multi-gpu, prefer keeping seq>192 on single GPU when possible to avoid cross-device kv coherence costs.
[03:58] Maya: on the on-prem security side, they asked about KMS and audit logs. Priya, is that a blocker for pilot?
[04:07] Priya: we need KMS + HSM option for key wrapping for PII, and we need request-level audit logs retained for 90 days.
[04:14] Maya: Redwood Private supports that; we'll hand you the compliance checklist after.
[04:19] Omar: back to kernel noise — do you have nvprof or nsight traces that map kernel names to decision points? We saw labels like "mha_fused_v2" and sometimes "attn_split_vIII" — not great naming consistency.
[04:31] Carlos: yes, we've attached a short set of nvtx-tagged traces. Note there's some mislabeling in open-source frontends, so we cross-reference with GPU hex ids. We'll share a mapping doc.
[04:44] [05:00] Speaker 1 (Priya): um quick question — is the graph invalidation unique to TRT-LLM or can vLLM also suffer?
[05:07] Carlos: vLLM can suffer if it tries to capture graphs for variable shapes; however vLLM's default tends to use more granular captures or no capture, which avoids wholesale invalidation but sacrifices the replay speed win. So it's a trade.
[05:23] Priya: what about quantization? We saw 4-bit sometimes causes hallucination-like logits drift, but latency was great.
[05:31] Carlos: quantization impacts both kernel choice and numerical stability. TRT-LLM's quant kernels are highly optimized but assume a certain layout; vLLM's int8/4-bit paths sometimes drop to emulated math which affects result. We recommend running a quality eval on your held-out prompts.
[05:48] Lena: is there an easy way to detect in prod when a kernel flip is about to happen so we can shard differently?
[05:54] Carlos: yes, heuristics: monitor KV cache size and recent sequence histogram; if you see a sudden percentile shift (p90->p99 increase) then trigger route change to a compatible kernel lane. Redwood runtime exposes these telemetry hooks.
[06:08] Omar: our main worry is nondeterministic spikes that happen during business hours. Can we force a lane to use a non-graph fallback for safety even if it's slower?
[06:17] Carlos: absolutely — you can pin a lane to immediate-mode kernels (no graph), which gives consistent latency at some throughput cost. For critical SLOs that's a common config.
[06:26] Priya: ok, how much throughput do we lose? ballpark?
[06:29] Carlos: depends — for short sequences you might lose 10-30% throughput vs a warmed TRT graph path; for long sequence fused kernels it can be higher. We'll provide numbers from our bench.
[06:41] Maya: we prepared a microbench — Carlos, can you summarize the key numbers from the run?
[06:47] Carlos: yeah, run details: model Llama-2-13B opt variant, two configs: TRT-LLM optimized with cudagraph replay and vLLM dynamic. Batch size 8 for latency-sensitive lanes. Seq profiles: 16/64/128/256 mixes. Results: TRT steady-state p50=18ms (seq16), p95=78ms (seq64), p99=310ms (seq256) when graphs stable. Intermixed workload caused reprogrep spikes up to 1.2s when graphs recompiled. vLLM p50=22ms, p95=95ms, p99=420ms but more stable under mix (rare >700ms events). Quantized 4-bit TRT gave p50=10ms but quality drop on some prompts.
[07:32] Priya: that 1.2s spike is exactly what we're seeing in prod sometimes.
[07:36] Carlos: yep. Recompile events typically show nvtx markers — we can detect and auto-failover to a pinned lane to dampen spikes.
[07:45] Lena: NVLink behavior? does cross-GPU KV sync cause extra invalidation?
[07:50] Carlos: cross-GPU introduces synchronization points, and if the kernel selector expects local contiguous memory it may flip to a different kernel or trigger an expensive all-reduce. For priming-heavy sessions, keeping the entire KV on a single GPU when the length is above threshold reduces kernel switching.
[08:06] Omar: that's tricky because we want to utilize multi-GPU for throughput. Any operational patterns?
[08:10] Carlos: common approach: two lanes — latency-critical lane pinned to single GPU with graph-capture tuned; throughput lane sharded across GPUs with dynamic kernels. Route requests by size and SLO.
[08:21] Priya: ok, actionability — what's the recommended pilot plan?
[08:24] Maya: Redwood proposes a 3-day pilot on your on-prem cluster: day 1 run sequence sweep, day 2 run mixed workload with traffic replay, day 3 run quantization A/B with quality evals. We'll provide the bench harness and scripts.
[08:36] Priya: sounds good. On security: how do we run the scripts without exposing data?
[08:40] Carlos: we ask for an anonymized prompt corpus and run via a short-lived service account; all artifacts are collected into your secure bucket. We can also run fully air-gapped if needed — Redwood Private supports an on-prem deploy with no external telemetry.
[08:54] [09:00] Omar: are there known kernel bugs in TRT-LLM builds that cause silent correctness issues on A800 vs A100?
[09:07] Carlos: some families had numerical corner cases on A800 with specific tile sizes under 4-bit quantization; we documented mitigations — avoid tile size X for int4 on that GPU, or use an emulated fallback with calibration. We'll attach those notes.
[09:24] Priya: are there any heuristics for when to prefer vLLM over TRT?
[09:29] Carlos: broadly: prefer TRT for stable, narrow shape workloads where you can amortize graph capture and where quantization quality is acceptable. Prefer vLLM if your workload is highly variable, low rate but high variance, and you want predictable tail behavior without graph recompiles.
[09:49] Lena: and cost-wise?
[09:53] Carlos: TRT often yields lower tokens-per-dollar in high-throughput steady-state. vLLM may be cheaper for scattered, low-throughput workloads because it avoids compile overhead and uses smaller working sets. But with dedicated reserved capacity you can tune that.
[10:07] Priya: one more — we saw kernel name "gemm_swizzle_v4" in traces; what's that?
[10:11] Carlos: oh that's a fused matmul-kernel specialized for certain dim tilings; it triggers for particular head counts and seq lengths. When it activates you see a big perf bump. But it's also fragile: small changes to quant layout or padding can switch it off.
[10:25] Omar: can Redwood runtime pin preference for that kernel?
[10:28] Carlos: we can set kernel-selection hints and schedule lanes to keep parameters that favor it. But it's a build-level heuristic; we can steer runtime but not force vendor binary internals.
[10:40] Priya: ok, let's talk observability — what logs/metrics should we collect to detect imminent graph invalidation?
[10:46] Carlos: collect: recent sequence length histogram, KV cache size, kernel-id timeline, nvtx compile markers, GPU memory high-watermarks, and graph replay failures. Redwood console surfaces an alert when compile rate > threshold.
[11:01] Maya: we'll provide you a template dashboard.
[11:04] Priya: do you have any quick wins we can apply now?
[11:07] Carlos: yes: 1) implement adaptive bucketing so batches are shape-consistent, 2) pin latency-critical workloads to immediate-mode kernels if tail spikes are unacceptable, 3) avoid aggressive int4 on A800 until you run calibration, 4) enable kernel-selection telemetry and set a rolling-compile rate alert.
[11:27] Lena: about calibration: how long does quant calibration take for our 13B model?
[11:32] Carlos: sample-based calibration can be done in a few hours on your infra for representative corpus; full sweep over many prompts is longer. We'll provide tooling to automate that.
[11:42] [12:00] Priya: if we go forward with pilot, do you need us to schedule downtime?
[12:06] Maya: no mandatory downtime; we'd prefer a fenced test pool or a maintenance window to reduce noise, but we can run in shadow mode.
[12:14] Omar: what's the expected deliverable from Redwood at pilot end?
[12:17] Maya: a benchmark report with p50/p95/p99 across buckets, kernel flip timeline, suggested runtime configs (bucketing, lane pins, quant profiles), and an operational runbook for graph compile monitoring.
[12:30] Priya: perfect. Two last quick technicals: 1) memory fragmentation due to frequent allocations — is that a known cause of kernel flip? 2) can we do pre-allocation strategies?
[12:38] Carlos: fragmentation can change available workspace and that will change selected kernels. Pre-allocating max workspace or using a memory pool mitigates flips. Redwood runtime supports a memory arena to reduce live malloc churn.
[12:53] Priya: great.
[12:55] Lena: any other risks?
[12:58] Carlos: watch out for scheduler jitter on shared infra and OS-level preemption — those can mimic kernel instability. Also watch the cuda driver version; mismatches sometimes change kernel heuristics.
[13:12] Maya: ok let's recap and next steps.
[13:15] Maya: action items — Carlos will prep bench scripts and kernel mapping, Priya uploads corpus, Maya shares security checklist and pilot statement of work. We'll schedule the pilot start for next week pending corpus.
[13:29] Priya: thanks everyone.
[13:31] Lena: thanks.
[13:33] Omar: thanks, bye.

Notes on transcript fidelity: some kernel names and markers are approximate; nvtx labels in customer's traces were noisy and required mapping. There's occasional filler words removed for readability but the transcript preserves decision points and timings.
